habitat: Open ocean and coastal waters worldwide
diet: Fish, squid, and crustaceans
funFacts: Dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time so they can keep breathing.
Each dolphin has a signature whistle that works like a name.
They can swim in bursts of over 30 km/h.

habitat: Shallow coral reefs and lagoons
diet: Small reef fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans
funFacts: Reef sharks often rest motionless on the sand by pumping water over their gills.
They are naturally cautious of large, unfamiliar movement.
Pups are born fully independent and receive no parental care.

habitat: Holes and crevices in coral reefs and wrecks
diet: Fish and octopus, hunted after dark
funFacts: The open mouth is not a threat — it has no gill covers, so it has to gape constantly to breathe.
A second set of jaws in its throat shoots forward to drag prey down, the only animal known to feed this way.
It hunts by smell, and reef fish will lead one to hidden prey and share the catch.

habitat: Warm coastal shelves, seamounts and reef drop-offs
diet: Fish, squid, and rays taken off the bottom
threats: Bycatch in longline and gillnet fisheries
funFacts: The wide head spreads their electrical sensors over a broader sweep, letting them find rays buried under the sand.
With an eye on each tip, a hammerhead can see all the way around itself from above and below at the same time.
They gather over seamounts in schools by day and split up to hunt alone at night.

habitat: Reef edges, wrecks and open water near structure
diet: Fish, taken in a single strike from ambush
threats: Overfishing of the reef fish it hunts
funFacts: It accelerates to around 58 km/h in a straight line — one of the fastest bursts of any fish.
The lower jaw sticks out past the upper one, so the teeth stay visible even when the mouth is shut.
Young ones travel in schools; a large adult usually hangs alone, motionless, and simply watches.

habitat: Tropical and subtropical seagrass beds and reefs
diet: Seagrass and algae (herbivorous as adults)
funFacts: Green sea turtles can hold their breath for several hours while resting.
They migrate thousands of kilometers between feeding and nesting grounds.
Their shell color comes from body fat tinted green by their algae diet.

habitat: Coral reefs, sheltering among sea anemones
diet: Algae, zooplankton, and small invertebrates
funFacts: Clownfish are immune to their host anemone's sting thanks to a protective mucus layer.
All clownfish are born male and can change sex to become the dominant female.
They rarely stray far from their home anemone.

habitat: Reef ledges, overhangs and wreckage
diet: Small fish and shrimp, cornered with the pectoral fans
threats: Aquarium collection in its native Indo-Pacific range
Reef degradation across the range it belongs to
funFacts: Eighteen of its fin rays are venomous spines — painful to a human, and the reason it never bothers to flee.
It herds small fish into a corner with its spread pectoral fans before swallowing them whole.
Released into the Atlantic by the aquarium trade, it now eats its way through reefs that have no defence against it.

habitat: Open coastal water, often in drifting swarms near the surface
diet: Zooplankton, fish eggs and larvae, and other jellyfish
funFacts: A sea nettle has no brain, no heart and no blood — only a net of nerves around the rim of its bell.
Its trailing tentacles can be several metres long behind a bell the width of a dinner plate.
It cannot swim against a current; the pulsing only moves it up and down, and the sea does the rest.

habitat: The midnight zone, below a thousand metres
diet: Whatever swims into the lure, up to twice its own size
threats: Changes in the sinking food supply from above
funFacts: The glowing lure is not its own light — it is a colony of bacteria the fish keeps and feeds.
Its skin reflects less than half a percent of the light that hits it, making it one of the blackest materials in nature.
Its stomach stretches far enough to swallow prey larger than itself, because a meal down here may be the last for months.

habitat: Open ocean worldwide, migrating between polar feeding and tropical breeding grounds
diet: Almost entirely krill, filtered through baleen plates
funFacts: The largest animal known to have ever lived — bigger than any dinosaur.
Its call carries for hundreds of kilometres and is louder than a jet engine.
A single mouthful can hold up to 80 cubic metres of water and krill.
Its heart alone weighs about as much as a small car.

habitat: Every ocean, from polar ice edges to the tropics
diet: Fish, seals, squid — diet varies sharply between populations
funFacts: Pods have their own dialects, passed down through generations.
Females can live past eighty and lead the pod long after they stop breeding.
Different populations hunt such different prey that they rarely interbreed.
The tall dorsal fin of an adult male can stand nearly two metres high.

habitat: Tropical and temperate open ocean, often near seamounts and reef cleaning stations
diet: Zooplankton and small fish, filtered while swimming
funFacts: Wingspans reach seven metres, making it the largest ray in the ocean.
It has the largest brain of any fish and appears to recognise itself in mirrors.
Each manta's belly spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.
It visits reef cleaning stations and waits for small fish to groom it.

habitat: Sandy flats, reef edges and lagoons in warm seas
diet: Clams, oysters and snails crushed with plated jaws
funFacts: It digs shellfish out of the sand with a snout shaped like a duck's bill, then crushes the shells with flat plates instead of teeth.
The white spots are unique to each animal, the way a fingerprint is.
It leaps clear of the surface and lands flat — nobody is certain why.

habitat: Rocky reefs and crevices in warm coastal water
diet: Crabs, shellfish and small fish
funFacts: An octopus can change both colour and skin texture in under a second.
Two thirds of its neurons are in its arms, so each arm partly thinks for itself.
It can squeeze through any gap wider than its beak — the only hard part of its body.
It keeps a den under a rock and piles the shells of everything it has eaten around the entrance — divers find the midden before they find the octopus.

habitat: Deep reef slopes and caverns of the tropical Pacific
diet: Carrion and moulted shells, found by smell
threats: Deep trapping for the ornament trade
funFacts: Its shell is divided into sealed chambers it floods and empties to control depth, like a submarine's ballast.
It has around ninety tentacles and not one of them has a sucker.
The eye is a pinhole with no lens at all — an open pit that fills with seawater.

habitat: Sand, seagrass and kelp in shallow coastal water
diet: Crabs, shrimp and small fish taken with two shooting tentacles
funFacts: It changes colour and texture in under a second, and it does this while being colour-blind.
The pupil is shaped like a W, which lets it judge distance without moving its head.
Inside is the cuttlebone — a gas-filled shell it fills and empties to hover without swimming.

habitat: Sandy and rocky seabeds down to the edge of the shelf
diet: Algae, molluscs and whatever it can scavenge
funFacts: Spider crabs pile into mounds thousands deep to moult in safety.
One claw is usually larger than the other, and it is not always the same side.
They decorate their shells with seaweed and sponge to disappear.

habitat: Cold seeps and hydrothermal vents on the deep sea floor
diet: Bacteria farmed on the bristles of its own claws
funFacts: The hair on its claws is a garden — it grows bacteria there and then combs them off and eats them.
It waves its claws through the chemical plume the way a farmer waters a crop.
It is blind, and it lives where sunlight has never reached, so the whole food chain around it runs on chemistry instead.

habitat: Rocky and sandy seabeds in shallow coastal water
diet: Mussels, clams and barnacles
funFacts: A sea star can regrow a lost arm, and some can regrow a whole body from one.
It eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and digesting prey outside itself.
It has no brain and no blood — it runs on seawater pumped through its body.

habitat: Cold coastal water, kelp beds and rocky shores
diet: Fish, squid and crustaceans
funFacts: A grey seal can hold its breath for well over twenty minutes.
Its whiskers track the wake a fish left behind, so it can hunt in total darkness.
Every seal's coat pattern is unique, which is how researchers tell them apart.

habitat: Antarctic pack ice and the water beneath it
diet: Fish, krill and squid caught on long dives
threats: Loss of the sea ice it breeds on
funFacts: It dives deeper than 500 metres and can stay under for over twenty minutes on one breath.
Underwater it flies — the flippers are stiff wings that beat against water instead of air.
Males incubate the single egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter, eating nothing for two months.

habitat: Warm open ocean, often near the surface
diet: Plankton and small fish, filtered from the water
funFacts: The largest fish alive, and it eats almost nothing bigger than your fingernail.
Every whale shark's pattern of spots is unique, so researchers identify them the way we use fingerprints.
It filters over six thousand litres of water an hour and never has to bite anything.

habitat: Open ocean, migrating between polar feeding grounds and warm breeding water
diet: Krill and small schooling fish
funFacts: Its flippers are nearly a third of its body length — the longest limbs of any animal alive.
Males sing songs that last twenty minutes and change a little every year, and every whale in an ocean sings the same one.
It blows a curtain of bubbles around a shoal of fish to herd them into a ball, then swims up through the middle.

habitat: Arctic waters and the leads between pack ice
diet: Halibut, cod and squid taken in deep winter dives
funFacts: The tusk is a single tooth that grows out through the upper lip, and it always spirals to the left.
It has no dorsal fin — a fin would catch on the ice it lives under, so it carries a low ridge instead.
The tusk is packed with nerve endings and appears to taste the water around it.

habitat: Blackwater and clearwater streams of the western Amazon basin
diet: Larvae, tiny crustaceans, and algae
threats: Deforestation and silt in Amazon headwaters
Acidification and pollution of blackwater streams
funFacts: The blue stripe is not a pigment. It is a layer of guanine crystals that scatters light, which is why it flares and dims as the fish turns.
They switch it off at night: the stripe fades to violet-grey while the fish sleeps, and comes back at first light.
Their home streams run the colour of strong tea, stained by tannins from the leaf litter of the flooded forest.
A shoal holds together by sight alone, so it scatters in the dark and re-forms at dawn.

habitat: Cool and temperate coastal waters, often near seal colonies
diet: Seals, sea lions, large fish, and carrion
funFacts: A great white keeps its body several degrees warmer than the sea around it, which lets it hunt in cold water.
It can sense the faint electrical fields of a hidden animal through jelly-filled pores in its snout.
Individuals cross entire ocean basins and return to the same coast years later.

habitat: Shallow sandy flats, kelp edges and estuaries
diet: Crabs, clam siphons, burrowing worms and small fish
funFacts: The leopard shark's saddle markings are unique to each animal, the way a fingerprint is.
It feeds by pushing its jaws out to suck prey from the sand rather than biting.
Large groups gather in warm shallows at high tide and disperse as the water drops.
